title: KV cache: Eviction backpressure and memory resilience playbook
creator: Aisha Khan
description: Follow-up to the 2026-02-08 degraded-serving incident where multiple hosts experienced sustained memory growth and cascading evictions. This ticket consolidates immediate mitigations, root cause analysis, and tracked engineering work to prevent recurrence and improve observability. Focus areas: eviction backpressure, slab fragmentation smoothing, iterator/reference leak detection, and targeted telemetry for early warning.
timeline: 2026-02-08 02:17 UTC: Alerts triggered - host group A memory > 92% and latency spike observed across low-latency routes.
2026-02-08 02:25 UTC: Initial mitigation - scaled out Dedicated pool and enabled emergency fallback to smaller model variant for affected routes.
2026-02-08 03:10 UTC: Engineering triage identified repetitive eviction storms correlated with concurrent high-insert workload and ongoing background iterators.
2026-02-09 10:40 UTC: Heap/profile samples collected; provisional hypothesis: fragmentation + retained iterator references slowing reclamation.
2026-02-10 09:00 UTC: Hotfix deployed - soft write-throttle applied per-namespace and eviction aggressiveness increased; memory growth stabilized.
2026-02-18 14:30 UTC: Detailed postmortem review; this ticket opened to track longer-term fixes and tests.
2026-02-20 11:05 UTC: Added action items and owners after eng + product review.
root_cause: Under high concurrent insert + iterate workloads, the eviction priority scoring amplified small transient differences (oscillation). This produced frequent small-object evictions that fragmented slabs and reduced effective free memory. Simultaneously, several iterator codepaths retained references longer than intended, delaying reclamation and preventing expected free-from-eviction. The runtime lacked a write-side backpressure mechanism, so producers kept pushing data until multiple hosts hit high watermark and eviction storms cascaded.
mitigations_applied: Deployed per-namespace soft write-throttle (token bucket) to slow producers when host memory > 80% - applied 2026-02-10
Increased eviction aggressiveness threshold temporarily to shed pressure while rollout stabilized
Enabled emergency route fallbacks to smaller model variant for the most impacted customers
long_term_actions: Implement eviction backpressure in runtime: token-bucket on write path with graceful 429 + retry guidance - owner: Miguel Torres - estimate: 3
Replace instantaneous eviction score with EWMA smoothing to avoid oscillation under bursty inserts - owner: Priya Patel - estimate: 5
Background slab compaction job to coalesce small free segments and reduce fragmentation; safe rate-limited ops during low-load windows - owner: Liam O'Connor - estimate: 8
Audit and harden iterator lifecycles: add debug-mode reference tracking, automatic finalizers for leaked iterators, and CI fuzz tests - owner: Sophie Zhang - estimate: 5
Add per-namespace soft quotas and emergency throttling policy in Smart Routing layer to avoid single tenant causing host-level pressure - owner: Miguel Torres - estimate: 3
Improve admission and fallback playbook in Console so SREs can trigger model route fallbacks and track affected tokens - owner: Product (Nina Brooks) - estimate: 2
validation_plan: Synthetic workload tests: high-concurrency insert + iterate pattern replay against staging clusters to reproduce previous memory growth curve
Chaos experiment: gradually increase write load until backpressure engages; verify latency and error surface match SLO targets
Regression suite: add memory-profiling harness to CI that fails on sustained >5% memory growth over 30min under stable qps
Nightly compaction smoke test to ensure background job does not induce latency spikes
monitoring_and_alerting_changes: Add evictions/sec and eviction-score-variance per-host and per-namespace to the default runtime dashboard
Create alert: sustained evictions/sec > 200 for >5min OR host free memory < 12% -> page on-call
Expose iterator-count and iterator-retained-refs metric; alert on unexpected growth
Add histogram of slab fragment sizes to detect fragmentation trends
